clue.text: Consult the cook

definitions.note: seethe in its old sense means to boil, so to cook

parts.note: to see a doctor or lawyer is to consult one

explanation.surface: An instruction to go and ask the chef for advice.
explanation.definitionFit: Seethe is an archaic verb for boiling food, a way of cooking it.

clue.text: Rents going up the whole year, like this ?

indicators.note: in a down clue going up reads the word for rents from bottom to top

parts.note: rips are rents or tears
all means the whole

explanation.surface: A complaint that rents keep climbing all year round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going up' turns RIPS into SPIR; prices rising ever upward suggest the spiral the definition points at.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirally means in a winding coil, the way spiralling rents climb.

clue.text: Looking green, six taken in by one rising American

indicators.note: taken in by means the six piece sits inside the reversed word for one
rising in a down clue means the word one reads upward, backwards

parts.note: taken as written
VI is six in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Someone appears sick and pale as six are swallowed by a lone upwardly mobile American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns ONE into ENO; 'taken in by' puts VI inside it, giving ENVIO.
explanation.definitionFit: Green is the colour of jealousy, so looking green means jealous.

clue.text: Cells filled by workers

parts.note: reads like prison cells crowded with labourers, but means wax cells stocked by worker bees

explanation.surface: Prison cells packed with labourers.
explanation.walkthrough: Worker bees fill wax cells with honey.
explanation.definitionFit: A bees' comb is a mass of hexagonal wax cells filled with honey by worker bees.

clue.text: Initially, should waste burn slowly?

indicators.note: initially means take only the opening letter of the word that follows, should

parts.note: to moulder is to waste away or decay

explanation.surface: A question about whether rubbish ought to be left to smoulder on a bonfire.
explanation.definitionFit: To smoulder is to burn with smoke but no flame, a slow fire.

clue.text: Underhand dealings in the pet shop

definitions.meaning: trickery or mischief is called this
taken literally, the trade in apes at a pet shop

explanation.surface: Shady trading going on at a pet shop.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means mischief or trickery, and literally a trade in primates such as a pet shop might carry on.

clue.text: Superior meal, but' no starter

indicators.note: no starter means the first letter of the meal word is dropped

parts.note: supper is an evening meal

explanation.surface: Someone complains of a fine dinner served without a first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starter' sounds like a first course, but it means the opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Upper means higher in rank, a synonym of superior.

clue.text: Hand up, I wave to the heir apparent

indicators.note: wave suggests the letters of hand up and I are shaken about

explanation.surface: Raising a hand, someone greets the prince who will be king.
explanation.walkthrough: The heir to the French throne was given this title.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dauphin was the title of the eldest son and heir of the King of France.

clue.text: 60% agree about place name

indicators.note: about means those three letters go round the word for place
sixty per cent of a five-letter word is three letters, here the closing three

parts.note: to put something is to place it

explanation.surface: A majority agree on a place name.
explanation.walkthrough: '60%' takes three of the five letters of AGREE, the last three, REE; 'about' wraps them round PUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A good name means a good reputation, standing in others' eyes.

clue.text: University administrator is wrong to risk mounting revolution …

parts.note: vice is wrongdoing
to chance something is to risk it

indicators.note: mounting in a down clue means the word for revolution climbs, so reads backwards

parts.note: a roll is a turn or revolution

explanation.surface: A university head is warned against gambling on a revolt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mounting' turns ROLL into LLOR. The ellipsis leads into 16 down.
explanation.definitionFit: In British universities this officer is the chief executive, below the titular chancellor.

clue.text: Born of one that knows no law

definitions.text: Born of one that knows no law

parts.words: Born of one that knows no law
parts.note: the proverb says necessity knows no law, and another says necessity is the mother of this, so it is born of necessity

explanation.surface: A description of a child of some lawless parent.
explanation.walkthrough: Two proverbs combine: 'Necessity knows no law' and 'Necessity is the mother of invention'.
explanation.definitionFit: A new contrivance is proverbially the offspring of necessity, the thing that knows no law.

clue.text: Fruit, soft and well-rounded

parts.note: a plum is a fruit
p (piano) is the musical abbreviation for soft

explanation.surface: A description of a ripe, soft, rounded fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: Plump describes a full, rounded figure, synonym of chubby.

clue.text: Has this drug done any wrong ?

indicators.note: wrong suggests the letters of done any are put the wrong way, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a medicine has caused any harm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' rearranges DONE ANY; the joke is that this soothing drug is the one meant to do no harm.
explanation.definitionFit: An anodyne is a painkilling medicine, a drug that soothes.

clue.text: Feel they're talking about you (out of this range)?

definitions.text: Feel they're talking about you (out of this range)?

parts.words: Feel they're talking about you (out of this range)?
parts.note: burning ears are said to show you are being talked about, and gossip happens beyond hearing distance

explanation.surface: Suspecting others are gossiping about you behind your back.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as EARS HOT: your ears burn when you are discussed, and gossips stay beyond the distance at which you could hear them.
explanation.definitionFit: Earshot is the range within which a voice can be heard; gossip happens outside it.

clue.text: Catch many a fool with love

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, a large number, so many
an ass is a fool
love is nil in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: Lots of silly people get caught up in romance.
explanation.walkthrough: L for 'many' is a crossword convention: any Roman numeral can stand for a large number.
explanation.definitionFit: A lasso is a looped rope used to catch cattle, and as a verb means to catch with one.

clue.text: Sinking about two blacks is somewhat lame

indicators.note: about means the word for sinking goes round the other piece

parts.note: holing a putt or a ball is sinking it
B is short for black, as on pencils, so two blacks give BB

explanation.surface: A snooker or golf player is poor at sinking the black balls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts BB inside HOLING. The snooker picture of potting black balls misleads: B is the pencil-grade abbreviation for black.
explanation.definitionFit: Hobbling means walking with a limp, partly lame.

clue.text: . he has licence to give in, in to revolutionaries' demand

indicators.note: in to means the word in is placed inside the slogan word

parts.note: liberté, liberty, was a demand of the French revolutionaries
taken as written

explanation.surface: Continuing 9 down: an official is licensed to yield to rebels' demands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'give in, in to' tells you to put IN into LIBERTE, the first word of the French revolutionary cry Liberté, égalité, fraternité.
explanation.definitionFit: A libertine is a man living with sexual licence, a dissolute rake.

clue.text: Failing 27

definitions.meaning: a failing is a fault or flaw
the answer to 27 across, meaning languor or tiredness

explanation.surface: A clue simply pointing at another answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a flaw in character, and a lack of strength like listlessness.

clue.text: Surgeon gave interview to Sanders' assistant

parts.note: to see someone is to grant them an interview
Bones (Lieutenant Tibbetts) is the assistant of Sanders in Edgar Wallace's Sanders of the River stories

explanation.surface: A doctor met a colonial commissioner's helper for an interview.
explanation.walkthrough: Edgar Wallace's Sanders of the River stories feature Commissioner Sanders and his young aide, Lieutenant Tibbetts, nicknamed Bones.
explanation.definitionFit: Sawbones is old slang for a surgeon, from bone-sawing amputations.

clue.text: Forgiveness from the little woman around the home

indicators.note: around means the name goes round the word for home

parts.note: Amy is one of the March sisters in Louisa May Alcott's Little Women
a nest is a home

explanation.surface: Pardon coming from a wife around the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the little woman' looks like a dated term for a wife, but points to Amy March of Alcott's novel Little Women.
explanation.definitionFit: An amnesty is an official pardon granted to offenders, a general forgiveness.

clue.text: Bead of, brass

definitions.meaning: a tube-shaped glass bead sewn on clothes
a brass instrument used for military calls

explanation.surface: A small ornament made of brass.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan prints 'of', so it reads as a link between the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a tubular glass dress bead, and the simple brass horn sounding military calls.

clue.text: Drop and break 20-look inside

indicators.note: inside means the word for look is placed in the 20 across answer
break suggests the combined letters are smashed and reassembled

parts.note: the answer to 20 across
lo is an old word meaning look

explanation.surface: A command to drop something and smash it, then peer in.
explanation.walkthrough: Put LO inside BUGLE (20 across) and 'break' rearranges all seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A globule is a small round drop of liquid.

clue.text: Take wrongly greeting to Mr Robinson

parts.note: hi is a greeting
Jack Robinson, as in the phrase 'before you could say Jack Robinson'

explanation.surface: Someone misreads a greeting addressed to a Mr Robinson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before you can say Jack Robinson' is an English idiom meaning very quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: To hijack is to seize a vehicle unlawfully, taking it wrongly.

clue.text: Though of low birth, somehow I belong to …

indicators.note: somehow says the letters of I belong are arranged in some other way

explanation.surface: Despite humble origins, the speaker claims membership of something named in the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs into 25 across, making 'I belong to Norfolk' a sentence across two clues.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignoble originally meant not of noble birth, so lowly born.

clue.text: It produces a prize-winning house

parts.note: reads like an award-winning builder, but the game where a full card wins with the call 'House!'

explanation.surface: A builder that makes award-winning homes.
explanation.walkthrough: In the British number game, a player who completes a card shouts 'House!' and wins a prize.
explanation.definitionFit: A numbers game where completing a card earns the cry 'House' and a prize.

clue.text: . the County, and not the common people

parts.note: nor means and not
folk are ordinary people

explanation.surface: Continuing the last clue: belonging to the upper-class county set, not the ordinary people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The County' plays on its sense of landed gentry; Norfolk is an English county in East Anglia.
explanation.definitionFit: Norfolk is a county of eastern England, an example of the definition.

clue.text: Vicar has no head for crime

indicators.note: no head means the first letter of the word for vicar is dropped

parts.note: a parson is a parish priest such as a vicar

explanation.surface: A clergyman lacks any aptitude for wrongdoing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no head' strips P from PARSON; 'head for crime' looks like a phrase about talent, but 'head' belongs with 'no'.
explanation.definitionFit: Arson, the deliberate setting of fires, is a criminal offence.

clue.text: Girl with charm, due in a way to languor

parts.note: a lass is a girl
it means sex appeal, a kind of charm

indicators.note: in a way suggests the letters of due are put in another order

explanation.surface: A charming girl puts her listlessness down to something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a way' rearranges DUE into UDE. IT for sex appeal comes from the 1920s 'It girl'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lassitude is weariness and lack of energy, a synonym of listlessness.

clue.text: Day broke strangely, it's noted

definitions.note: a definition phrased as a description: the thing that has notes

indicators.note: strangely signals that the letters of day broke are set out oddly

explanation.surface: Dawn came in an odd way, someone remarks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's noted' looks like a comment on the strange dawn, but describes something with musical notes, as on a piano.
explanation.definitionFit: A piano's row of keys each sound a musical note, so it carries notes.

clue.text: Rebecca was one' we observed in Mr Oakroyd's embrace

definitions.note: a description standing for a noun: what Rebecca was

indicators.note: embrace means the name of Mr Oakroyd wraps around the other piece

parts.note: Jess Oakroyd is a character in J. B. Priestley's The Good Companions

explanation.surface: A character is described by someone watching another hold her.
explanation.walkthrough: Rebecca is the Jewish heroine of Scott's Ivanhoe; Jess Oakroyd is a Yorkshireman in Priestley's The Good Companions.
explanation.definitionFit: Rebecca in Walter Scott's Ivanhoe is a Jewish woman, the old word for which this is.
